sequence._describe: The crew gathered at the judging ring's edge in the morning, Gideon freshly brushed and pleased with himself, Widow Tillet arriving with an even more spectacularly groomed Bartholomew across the ring. Gideon and Bartholomew are both large, sturdy adult goats (roughly 32 inches/80cm at the shoulder) - Gideon plain grey and sturdy, Bartholomew a groomed creamy/golden-brown show goat. Warm painterly storybook illustration style, expressive and slightly exaggerated proportions, rich saturated color, soft painterly brushwork, comedic tone. Wide shot, 3:2 landscape aspect ratio, bright morning festival lighting, anticipatory comedic mood.

text: Morning arrived considerably too early for anyone's taste, and found the whole group gathered at the judging ring's edge, Gideon freshly brushed by an over-enthusiastic festival volunteer and looking, if anything, more pleased with the arrangement than he had the day before.
“He's going to win,” Grimalkin said, with the flat certainty of a cat who had already decided how the morning would go. “Look at him. He's already decided he's won.”
“I hope he does,” Barley said. “Though I also hope the other one does. I don't like anyone losing anything. It seems unfair to whoever loses.”
“That's not how competitions work, Barley.”
“I know. I still don't like it.”
Marian, watching the judges take their positions, allowed herself a small, tired smile. “Let's just get through this,” she said, “and go home.”

Widow Tillet arrived shortly after, Bartholomew groomed to an even more spectacular degree than the previous day, and took her position across the ring with the particular grim focus of a woman who had, evidently, spent the previous evening steeling herself for exactly this moment.
“May the better goat win,” she said, to Marian, in a tone that suggested she had already decided which one that would be.

“May the better goat win,” Marian agreed, evenly, and found, somewhat to her own surprise, that she meant it without any particular anxiety attached — whatever happened this morning, they were going home with Gideon regardless, ribbon or no ribbon.

sequence._describe: Gideon and Bartholomew both performing excellently before two head judges and a nervous assistant, the judges conferring with visible distress unable to decide, the crowd watching intently. Warm painterly storybook illustration style, expressive and slightly exaggerated proportions, rich saturated color, soft painterly brushwork, comedic tone. Wide shot, 3:2 landscape aspect ratio, tense comedic daytime judging lighting, suspenseful mood.

text: The judging, when it finally began, proved considerably more thorough than any of them had anticipated — coat condition, temperament, bearing, a bewildering array of criteria that two head judges and a visibly nervous assistant worked through with real, painstaking seriousness while the assembled crowd watched with the rapt attention generally reserved for considerably higher-stakes affairs.

Gideon performed magnificently, holding his position with calm, unbothered dignity through every inspection. Bartholomew, for his part, performed just as magnificently, clearly a creature who had done this many times before and knew exactly how to make the most of every angle.
“They're evenly matched,” Robin murmured, watching the judges confer with increasing, visible distress. “I don't think they know what to do.”

The head judge, after a conference that ran considerably longer than the festival's schedule had allotted for it, finally straightened, cleared his throat, and delivered his verdict with the particular careful diplomacy of a man determined not to start a local feud over livestock.

“After considerable deliberation,” he announced, “the judges find themselves unable to separate this year's two finest entries on any meaningful point of merit. We are, for the first time in this festival's history, declaring joint champions.”

A murmur of surprise rippled through the crowd. Widow Tillet's face did something complicated — disappointment, certainly, but underneath it, something that looked almost like relief at not having actually lost.
“Well,” she said, to no one in particular. “That's one way to settle it.”

sequence._describe: Widow Tillet overhearing Robin of Loxby speaking tenderly to Gideon while adjusting a ribbon, her expression softening with quiet understanding, Marian Fletcher standing nearby. Warm painterly storybook illustration style, expressive and slightly exaggerated proportions, rich saturated color, soft painterly brushwork, comedic tone. Wide shot, 3:2 landscape aspect ratio, warm gentle daytime lighting, tender emotional mood.

text: It was afterward, once the crowd had thinned and the ribbons had been distributed with equal ceremony to both animals, that Widow Tillet found herself lingering near enough to overhear Will speaking quietly to Gideon, adjusting the goat's second, freshly-awarded ribbon with real, unselfconscious affection.

“You gave us quite a fright, you know,” he was saying. “We don't just keep you around because you're useful. You do understand that, don't you? You're part of this whole ridiculous family, same as any of us.”
Widow Tillet, listening, felt something in her carefully maintained composure shift, just slightly.
“He talks to that goat like it's kin,” she said, to Marian, not entirely unkindly.
“He talks to all of them like that,” Marian said. “We all do. It's rather the whole point of keeping them.”

“I've had Bartholomew eleven years,” Widow Tillet said, after a moment, something considerably softer in her voice than it had carried since her arrival. “Buried a husband in that time. Lost most of the family I started with. He's rather all I've got left that greets me properly of a morning.” She looked at Gideon, then at Robin, with an expression that had shed nearly all of yesterday's hostility. “I suppose I understood that about your lot before I let myself admit it. That's why I fought so hard to keep him from you, more than the ribbon ever mattered. Didn't want to imagine losing that kind of thing myself.”
“You're not losing anything,” Marian said, gently. “We're simply taking home what's ours. There was never any real contest between what either of us stood to lose.”
Widow Tillet, for the first time since her arrival, offered something that might genuinely have been called a smile.

sequence._describe: Robin of Loxby confronting the crew about the invented nonsense cant terms, Will Scarlett-Sleeves caught guilty, Long John Little grinning, Brother Crumb reaching for food diplomatically. Warm painterly storybook illustration style, expressive and slightly exaggerated proportions, rich saturated color, soft painterly brushwork, comedic tone. Wide shot, 3:2 landscape aspect ratio, warm daytime lighting, playful confrontational mood.

text: It was on the walk back toward the festival's edge, coin and ribbon and considerable dignity all more or less intact, that Robin finally turned to the assembled group with the particular expression of a man who had spent an entire day quietly doing arithmetic nobody had noticed him doing.

“Bishop's bonnet doesn't rhyme with elephant,” he said. “Turnip's cousin doesn't rhyme with tomorrow either. And I've heard hound's-tooth and widow's-mite and beggar's-cloak enough times now to know the actual pattern, and neither of those follow it at all.”
Will opened his mouth, visibly searching for a defense, and found, after a moment, that he didn't actually have one.
“You've been making half of it up,” Robin said. “This whole time.”

“Some of it,” Marian admitted, entirely without shame. “Not all of it. We wouldn't lie about the real ones. Just... supplemented, occasionally, when the real ones weren't quite entertaining enough on their own.”

Robin looked at all of them — Marian's unrepentant calm, Will's guilty half-smile, Long John's poorly-concealed grin, Brother Crumb already reaching for something to eat as a diplomatic distraction — and felt, rather to his own surprise, the beginnings of a laugh he couldn't quite hold back.
“An elephant,” he said, shaking his head. “I nearly believed you. I actually, properly considered that might be real.”
“That's rather what made it fun,” Marian said, warmly, relieved to see him laughing rather than genuinely aggrieved. “You're too honest a man to expect deception. It made you an excellent audience.”
“I don't know whether to be flattered or insulted.”
“Both,” said Will, cheerfully. “Always both, with us.”

They walked home slowly, Gideon trotting ahead with two ribbons now pinned to his rope and an expression of purest, unbothered satisfaction, and behind him, for the first time in a full day, the whole camp laughed together — Robin loudest of all, finally, properly in on the joke.
